title: Board Governance and Policy
subtitle: Plain starting points for the policies a church needs before a crisis forces it to write one in a hurry.
intro:
Most churches write their first real policy the week after they wish they already had it. A child gets hurt, a count comes up short, a staff complaint lands in someone's lap, and suddenly the board is drafting in the dark under pressure and grief. This library exists so you are not starting from nothing on the worst day.

Every template here is a starting point and not finished law. They are written plainly so a small board can actually read and use them, but they are not legal advice and they are not a substitute for it. Your state, your denomination, your insurance carrier, and your local counsel all have requirements that this library cannot know.

So take what follows as a first draft to think against, not a form to sign. Adapt every one of these to your own context, your own polity, and your own law before you adopt it. The safeguarding policies in particular must be shaped by professionals, because there the cost of getting it wrong is a child.

categories.name: Foundational Governance
categories.blurb: The bare structure of how the church decides, who holds authority, and how the board actually functions.

policies.name: Bylaws Essentials
policies.why: Bylaws are the rules the church has agreed to govern itself by, and a church without clear ones ends up settling every dispute by whoever argues loudest or remembers the most history. Good bylaws name who has authority, how leaders are chosen and removed, how members join, and how the church amends its own rules. When conflict comes, and it will, the bylaws are what keep a disagreement from becoming a split. Courts and insurers will also look to them, so vague or contradictory bylaws can cost the church far more than a hard conversation would have.
policies.sample:
BYLAWS OF [Church Name]
Adopted [Date]

Article I. Name and Purpose
The name of this church is [Church Name]. Its purpose is to worship God, make disciples of Jesus Christ, and serve its community in accordance with [Statement of Faith reference].

Article II. Affiliation
This church is [independent / affiliated with [Denomination]].

Article III. Membership
Membership is defined in the Membership Policy adopted by the board. Members in good standing may vote at duly called members meetings.

Article IV. Governance
The governing board of this church is the [Board / Elders / Council], consisting of [number] members serving [length] terms. The board holds authority for [list, for example doctrine, budget, hiring of senior staff, property].

Article V. Officers
The officers are [Chair, Treasurer, Secretary], elected by [the board / the membership] for terms of [length].

Article VI. Meetings
A regular members meeting shall be held at least [annually]. Special meetings may be called by [Role] with [number] days written notice. A quorum is [number or percentage] of members in good standing.

Article VII. Amendments
These bylaws may be amended by a [two-thirds] vote of members present at a meeting where the amendment was given in writing at least [number] days in advance.

[Adapt all bracketed items to your polity and confirm with local counsel before adoption.]

policies.name: Board Roles and Responsibilities
policies.why: When everyone on a board is responsible for everything, no one is actually responsible for anything, and the work falls on whoever feels guiltiest. Naming the roles and what each one owns keeps the board from both neglecting duties and stepping on each other. It also protects individual members, because a board member who knows the scope of the role is far less likely to take on personal liability by acting alone. Clear roles are the difference between a board that governs and a committee that meets.
policies.sample:
BOARD ROLES AND RESPONSIBILITIES
[Church Name], adopted [Date]

The Board as a whole is responsible for the spiritual oversight, legal compliance, financial integrity, and strategic direction of [Church Name]. Individual board members hold no authority acting alone except as the board delegates in writing.

Chair
Leads board meetings, sets the agenda with staff input, ensures decisions are carried out, and speaks for the board when authorized.

Treasurer
Oversees financial records and reporting, ensures the financial controls policy is followed, presents budgets and statements to the board, and works with any independent reviewer.

Secretary
Keeps accurate minutes of all board and members meetings, maintains official records and policies, and ensures required filings are tracked.

All Members
Prepare for and attend meetings, keep confidential matters confidential, declare conflicts of interest, support decisions of the board once made, and complete any required safeguarding training.

Term and Removal
Members serve [length] terms. A member may be removed for [cause, for example disqualifying conduct or sustained absence] by a [two-thirds] vote, following the process in the bylaws.

[Adapt roles to your governance model and confirm with local counsel.]

policies.name: Decision-Making and Meetings
policies.why: A church that has never agreed how it makes decisions will discover the hard way that it has no agreed way to make decisions, usually in the middle of a fight. A simple policy on quorums, notice, voting thresholds, and minutes prevents a small group from making large decisions quietly and prevents one loud meeting from overturning months of work. Written minutes in particular protect the church, because a decision no one recorded is a decision someone will later remember differently.
policies.sample:
DECISION-MAKING AND MEETINGS POLICY
[Church Name], adopted [Date]

Regular Meetings
The board meets [monthly] at a time set at the start of each year. Staff and guests may attend by invitation.

Notice and Agenda
An agenda is circulated at least [number] days before each meeting. Items not on the agenda may be discussed but major decisions should be deferred unless [number] of members agree to act.

Quorum
A quorum is [a majority] of current board members. No binding decision may be made without a quorum present.

Voting
Ordinary decisions pass by [a majority] of members present. The following require a [two-thirds] vote: [budget adoption, hiring or releasing senior staff, property decisions, policy adoption, doctrinal matters].

Minutes
The Secretary records attendance, motions, votes, and decisions for every meeting. Minutes are approved at the next meeting and kept as a permanent record.

Confidentiality
Sensitive personnel, financial, and pastoral matters discussed in closed session remain confidential to the board.

[Adapt thresholds and structure to your bylaws and polity.]

categories.name: Finance and Money
categories.blurb: How the church handles the money it is trusted with, so that no one is ever alone with it and no one is ever falsely accused.

policies.name: Counting and Handling Offerings
policies.why: Most church embezzlement is not done by a thief who came in to steal but by a trusted member who was left alone with the money one too many times. A counting policy protects the funds and protects the people, because the person who is never alone with the offering can never be accused of taking it. Two unrelated counters, immediate documentation, and prompt deposit are the simplest and most important financial controls a church can adopt, and they cost nothing but discipline.
policies.sample:
OFFERING COUNTING AND HANDLING POLICY
[Church Name], adopted [Date]

Purpose
To protect the church's funds and the reputation of everyone who handles them, no person is ever alone with uncounted offerings.

Counting Team
Offerings are counted by at least two unrelated people from a rotating team. People who live in the same household do not count together. The [Treasurer / paid bookkeeper] does not count alone.

Process
1. Offerings are secured immediately after collection and kept in view until counting begins.
2. The team counts together, records the total on a count sheet, and both counters sign it.
3. Cash and checks are recorded separately. Designated gifts are noted by fund.
4. Funds are deposited within [one business day] or secured in a locked safe until deposit.
5. The count sheet is given to the [Treasurer] and reconciled against the bank deposit by a different person.

Records
Count sheets and deposit records are kept for [retention period per local requirement].

[Confirm retention periods and any local requirements with your accountant or counsel.]

policies.name: Expense Approval and Spending Authority
policies.why: Without spending limits, every purchase becomes a judgment call and every staff member is one impulse away from a decision that embarrasses the church. Clear thresholds say who can spend what without further approval, what needs a second signature, and what has to come to the board. This protects the church from both fraud and honest overreach, and it protects staff from the suspicion that follows unclear authority. It also keeps the board out of the weeds of small purchases so it can watch the large ones.
policies.sample:
EXPENSE APPROVAL AND SPENDING AUTHORITY POLICY
[Church Name], adopted [Date]

Budgeted Spending
Expenses within the approved annual budget may be authorized as follows:
Up to [amount]: [Staff role] may approve.
Up to [amount]: [Senior pastor / executive role] may approve.
Above [amount]: requires board approval.

Unbudgeted Spending
Any expense not in the approved budget over [amount] requires board approval regardless of urgency, except genuine emergencies, which must be reported to the board at the next meeting.

Dual Control
No single person may both approve and pay an expense to themselves. Reimbursements to a staff or board member are approved by someone other than that person.

Payments
Checks or transfers over [amount] require [two signatures / dual authorization]. Use of any church card follows the [card use policy] and requires itemized receipts.

Documentation
Every expense requires a receipt and a stated purpose. Missing documentation is treated as personal until resolved.

[Set dollar thresholds to your size and confirm with your accountant.]

policies.name: Benevolence Fund Policy
policies.why: Benevolence is where a church's compassion meets its accountability, and without a policy it becomes either an open spigot or an awkward favor decided in a hallway. A written policy sets who can request help, who decides, what limits apply, and how it is documented, which protects both the people asking and the people deciding. It also keeps the fund within the rules that let it remain charitable rather than becoming taxable personal gifts, which is a real risk that quiet, undocumented giving can create.
policies.sample:
BENEVOLENCE FUND POLICY
[Church Name], adopted [Date]

Purpose
The benevolence fund exists to provide short-term help to people facing genuine hardship, as an expression of the church's care, within the church's means and the law.

Who May Request
Anyone may request help. Priority is given as the [committee / pastor] discerns need. The church does not promise assistance and decisions are made case by case.

Decision and Limits
Requests up to [amount] may be approved by [role]. Requests above [amount] require [committee / board] approval. Help to any household is generally limited to [amount or frequency] within [period], with exceptions noted in writing.

How Help Is Given
Whenever possible, payments are made directly to the provider, such as a landlord or utility, rather than as cash to the individual. The church controls the use of all benevolence funds and does not act as a pass-through for designated gifts to a specific person.

Documentation and Confidentiality
Each request records the need, the decision, the amount, and the recipient, kept confidentially. Records are retained for [period].

[Designated gifts to a named individual may not be tax-deductible. Confirm benevolence practices with a qualified accountant or counsel.]

policies.name: Annual Financial Review
policies.why: A church that never has an outside set of eyes on its books is trusting that nothing has gone wrong and that nothing will, which is a heavy bet to place on the honesty of one person and the attention of a tired board. An annual review or audit, scaled to the church's size, catches errors, deters fraud, and gives the congregation a true picture of where its money went. It is also the clearest way to honor the people who gave, by proving their gifts were handled with care.
policies.sample:
ANNUAL FINANCIAL REVIEW POLICY
[Church Name], adopted [Date]

Purpose
To give the board and congregation independent assurance that the church's finances are handled with integrity.

Scope
Each year the church arranges a financial review appropriate to its size. This may be:
- An external audit by a licensed accountant, or
- A review engagement by an accountant, or
- An internal review by a committee of [number] members who are not signers on church accounts and do not handle money.

What Is Reviewed
The reviewer examines bank reconciliations, a sample of expenses and supporting receipts, payroll and tax filings, the counting records, and compliance with the church's own financial policies.

Reporting
Findings and any recommendations are presented in writing to the board and summarized for the congregation at the [annual meeting].

Independence
No person reviews their own work. The [Treasurer] and any paid bookkeeper do not conduct the review.

[Some states and lenders require a specific level of review. Confirm requirements with your accountant or counsel.]

categories.name: Safeguarding and Protection
categories.blurb: The policies that protect children and the vulnerable, where getting it wrong is not a paperwork problem but a person.

policies.name: Child and Youth Protection Policy
policies.why: Every church believes abuse could not happen here until it does, and the churches that are devastated by it are almost always the ones that trusted reputation instead of structure. A child protection policy is not an insult to your volunteers, it is a wall around the children and a shield for the innocent, because clear rules protect good workers from false suspicion as surely as they deter predators. This is the single most important policy in this library, and it is the one you must build with professional help, not from a template alone.
policies.sample:
CHILD AND YOUTH PROTECTION POLICY
[Church Name], adopted [Date]

This is a starting framework only. Before adopting any safeguarding policy, [Church Name] must consult its insurance carrier, local counsel, and a qualified child protection professional, and must follow all applicable local, state, and federal law. Where this template and the law differ, the law governs.

Commitment
[Church Name] is committed to the safety of every child and youth in its care and to protecting them from all forms of abuse.

Screening
Everyone who works with minors, paid or volunteer, completes an application, an interview, reference checks, and a background check, and observes a waiting period of [period] as a member before serving. See the Background Check Policy.

The Two-Adult Rule
No adult is ever alone with a child out of sight of another approved adult. Restrooms, transportation, and one-on-one meetings follow the procedures in this policy. Doors have windows or stay open.

Training
All workers complete safeguarding training before serving and refresh it [annually]. Training covers recognizing, preventing, and reporting abuse.

Reporting
Anyone who suspects a child has been abused must report to civil authorities as required by law. See the Abuse Reporting Policy. Suspected abuse is never handled internally in place of reporting.

Review
This policy is reviewed [annually] with professional input.

[Do not adopt this without professional and legal review. Mandatory reporting law applies regardless of what any church policy says.]

policies.name: Background Check Policy
policies.why: A background check is the most basic act of due diligence a church can take, and skipping it because someone is well liked is exactly how known offenders end up with access to children. Checks are not a guarantee, because most abuse never reaches a record, which is why they work alongside screening and the two-adult rule rather than in place of them. But a documented check on every worker shows that the church took reasonable care, which protects children first and the church second, and the absence of one is hard to defend after harm is done.
policies.sample:
BACKGROUND CHECK POLICY
[Church Name], adopted [Date]

This policy must conform to applicable law and to your insurer's requirements. Consult counsel and your carrier before adopting it, because background check law varies by jurisdiction and is strictly regulated.

Who Is Checked
Every paid staff member and every volunteer who works with minors or vulnerable adults, handles money, or holds a position of trust completes a background check before serving and is rechecked every [period].

What Is Checked
Checks include [criminal records, sex offender registry, and other screening as advised by counsel and your carrier]. Checks are conducted through [approved provider] with the person's written consent.

Results and Decisions
Results are reviewed confidentially by [designated role(s)]. A disqualifying result for work with minors includes [any offense against a child or as advised by counsel]. Decisions are documented and the reasons kept confidential.

Confidentiality
Results are stored securely, accessible only to [designated roles], and never disclosed beyond what the law and the decision require.

Fairness
The church follows all legal requirements for consent, notice, and the rights of applicants when a record affects a decision.

[Background screening is regulated by law. Do not adopt or act on checks without legal guidance.]

policies.name: Abuse Reporting Policy
policies.why: When a child discloses abuse or a worker suspects it, the people in the room are usually frightened, untrained, and tempted to handle it quietly to protect the church or to be sure before involving anyone. That instinct is wrong and it is dangerous. The law in most places requires immediate reporting to civil authorities, often by anyone who suspects, and the church's job is to report and protect, not to investigate or to decide whether the suspicion is strong enough. A clear policy removes the hesitation in the moment that matters most.
policies.sample:
ABUSE REPORTING POLICY
[Church Name], adopted [Date]

This policy must be reviewed against your local mandatory reporting law, which overrides anything written here. In many places, any person who suspects child abuse is legally required to report it. Confirm your jurisdiction's rules with counsel and your local child protection authority.

The Standard
The safety of the child comes before the reputation of the church or any person. We report suspected abuse. We do not investigate it ourselves and we do not decide internally whether it is true before reporting.

What To Do
1. If a child is in immediate danger, call emergency services now.
2. Anyone who suspects or learns of abuse reports it to the civil authorities as required by law, within the time the law requires. Do not wait for permission from a leader.
3. Notify [designated leader] so the church can cooperate, support the child and family, and meet its own obligations. Notifying a leader never replaces reporting to authorities.
4. Preserve any evidence and write down what was seen or said as soon as possible.
5. Do not confront the alleged offender, do not question the child beyond their first disclosure, and do not promise secrecy.

Care and Cooperation
The church cooperates fully with authorities, supports the affected child and family, and follows its insurer's and counsel's guidance on communication.

No Internal Resolution
Under no circumstances does the church handle suspected abuse internally in place of reporting to civil authorities.

[Mandatory reporting law governs. When in doubt, report. Confirm specifics with local authorities and counsel.]

categories.name: Personnel
categories.blurb: How the church treats the people it employs, so that fairness is written down before a hard situation tests it.

policies.name: Staff Handbook Essentials
policies.why: A staff handbook is how a church says in advance how it will treat its people, instead of inventing the answer under pressure when someone is hurt or angry. It sets expectations for both sides, covers the basics of hours, pay, leave, and conduct, and gives a small church a consistent way to act so that two employees in the same situation are treated the same. Without one, every personnel question becomes a one-off negotiation, and the staff member with the least power usually loses.
policies.sample:
STAFF HANDBOOK ESSENTIALS
[Church Name], adopted [Date]

This handbook describes how [Church Name] works with its employees. It is not a contract of employment and does not change the at-will or other status defined by [your jurisdiction and counsel].

Employment
We describe each role in a written job description. [State at-will or contract status as advised by counsel.]

Hours and Pay
Regular hours, pay periods, and overtime follow [applicable wage law]. Ministerial and non-ministerial roles are classified as advised by counsel.

Time Off
The church provides [vacation, sick leave, holidays, and parental or bereavement leave] as set out in [schedule]. Requests follow [process].

Conduct
Staff are expected to uphold the church's statement of faith and standards of conduct, treat others with respect, and avoid harassment of any kind. Concerns are raised through the Grievance Policy.

Confidentiality
Staff protect the privacy of members, givers, and pastoral matters.

Reviews and Discipline
Each role receives a [annual] review. Discipline follows a fair and documented process, except where conduct requires immediate action.

Safeguarding
All staff complete safeguarding training and follow the protection policies.

[Employment law varies widely. Have counsel review the handbook before adoption.]

policies.name: Conflict of Interest Policy
policies.why: Conflicts of interest are rarely about bad people, they are about good people who did not see how a decision touched them until someone outside the room did. A policy that requires leaders to declare conflicts and step back from those decisions protects the church from self-dealing and protects honest leaders from the appearance of it. It is also expected by many insurers and required for many tax filings, so having one in place is both wise stewardship and a practical safeguard for the church's standing.
policies.sample:
CONFLICT OF INTEREST POLICY
[Church Name], adopted [Date]

Purpose
To protect the church's decisions from being influenced, or appearing to be influenced, by the private interests of those who make them.

Who It Covers
All board members, officers, and staff who take part in church decisions.

What Is a Conflict
A conflict exists when a person, or their family member or business, could benefit from a church decision, or when loyalties could improperly affect their judgment. Examples include hiring a relative, buying from a board member's company, or setting one's own compensation.

Duty to Disclose
Anyone with a possible conflict declares it as soon as they recognize it, before discussion of the matter.

Handling the Conflict
The person with the conflict leaves the room for the discussion and the vote, does not influence it, and the minutes record the disclosure and the recusal. Compensation for any leader is set by others, never by the person being paid.

Annual Statement
Each covered person signs a conflict of interest statement [annually] disclosing known conflicts.

[Confirm this meets your tax and corporate requirements with counsel or your accountant.]

policies.name: Grievance and Complaint Policy
policies.why: When a staff member or volunteer is mistreated and has no clear way to raise it, the complaint does not disappear, it goes underground and comes back larger, often as a resignation, a rumor, or a lawsuit. A grievance policy gives people a known and safe path to be heard, sets out how complaints are handled and by whom, and forbids retaliation. It protects the vulnerable person who needs to speak and it protects the church by surfacing problems while they are still small enough to solve.
policies.sample:
GRIEVANCE AND COMPLAINT POLICY
[Church Name], adopted [Date]

Purpose
To give every staff member and volunteer a fair and safe way to raise a concern and to have it taken seriously.

Scope
This policy covers workplace concerns such as unfair treatment, harassment, unsafe conditions, or breaches of church policy. Suspected abuse follows the Abuse Reporting Policy instead and is reported to authorities.

How To Raise a Concern
1. Where safe and appropriate, raise it first with your direct supervisor.
2. If that is not appropriate, or is unresolved, bring it in writing to [designated role, for example board chair or a personnel committee].
3. A concern about the senior pastor or that role goes directly to [the board chair or personnel committee].

How It Is Handled
The church acknowledges the concern within [number] days, looks into it fairly and confidentially as far as possible, and gives a written outcome within [number] days. Both sides are heard.

No Retaliation
No one who raises a concern in good faith will face retaliation. Retaliation is itself a violation of this policy.

[Have counsel confirm this fits your employment law and any required complaint procedures.]

categories.name: Membership and Discipline
categories.blurb: How people belong, how they are restored, and how the church handles sin among its own with the seriousness and gentleness Jesus required.

policies.name: Membership Policy
policies.why: Membership is how a church says who has covenanted to belong to it and to be cared for and accountable within it, and a church with no clear membership has no clear answer to who votes, who is shepherded, and who the leaders are responsible for. Defining how a person becomes a member, what membership asks of them, and how it ends keeps belonging from being either meaningless or arbitrary. It also gives the discipline and restoration process its footing, because you cannot restore someone to a body they were never clearly part of.
policies.sample:
MEMBERSHIP POLICY
[Church Name], adopted [Date]

What Membership Is
Membership is a covenant relationship in which a believer commits to this local church and the church commits to shepherd and walk with them.

Becoming a Member
A person becomes a member by:
1. A credible profession of faith in Jesus Christ and baptism [as your tradition holds].
2. Completing [a membership class or conversation].
3. Affirming the church's statement of faith and membership covenant.
4. Being received by [the board / the congregation].

What Members Commit To
Members commit to gather with the church, support its work and ministry, pursue holiness, submit to its loving care and correction, and seek peace within the body.

What the Church Commits To
The church commits to teach and shepherd its members, pray for them, care for them in need, and pursue them in restoration if they fall.

When Membership Ends
Membership ends by death, by transfer or written request to resign, by joining another church, or through the church discipline process. A request to resign while under discipline is handled by [the board] in line with the Discipline Policy.

[Adapt to your polity and tradition and confirm with counsel where membership affects voting or property rights.]

policies.name: Church Discipline Process
policies.why: Church discipline has been so often abused or so often ignored that many churches have quietly dropped it, which leaves them unable either to confront real sin or to do it without harm when they finally must. A plain process built on the steps Jesus gave keeps discipline from becoming a weapon of the powerful or a humiliation of the weak. It moves from private and gentle toward public only as needed, it aims always at restoration rather than punishment, and it gives the church a path that is both faithful to Scripture and defensible if it is ever questioned.
policies.sample:
CHURCH DISCIPLINE PROCESS
[Church Name], adopted [Date]

Purpose
The aim of discipline is always restoration, never punishment or shame. We follow the pattern of Matthew 18 with gentleness, patience, and confidentiality, keeping each step as private as faithfulness allows.

Step One, Private
The person who sees a brother or sister in serious, unrepented sin goes to them privately, in humility, seeking to win them back. Most matters end here.

Step Two, One or Two More
If there is no repentance, the person returns with one or two others who can help confirm the facts and call for restoration.

Step Three, The Leaders
If there is still no repentance, the matter is brought to [the elders / board], who examine it carefully and continue the call to repentance with patience.

Step Four, The Church
Only if a member persists in serious, unrepented sin after these steps, and the leaders agree, is the matter brought to the church, which lovingly affirms the seriousness of the sin and the removal from membership, while continuing to pray for and seek the person.

Guardrails
This process is never used over disputable matters or personal offense that should be forgiven. Any matter involving suspected crime, abuse, or danger is reported to civil authorities first and is not handled as internal discipline. Confidentiality is kept at every step.

[Confirm with counsel, especially regarding any public communication about a member, defamation risk, and the absolute priority of reporting crimes to authorities.]

policies.name: Restoration Policy
policies.why: A church that knows how to confront sin but not how to welcome the repentant back has only learned half of what Jesus taught, and people sense it, which is part of why the wandering rarely return. A restoration policy names how someone moves from repentance back toward full fellowship, with grace and with wisdom about trust that has to be rebuilt over time. It guards against both a cheap restoration that ignores real harm and a cruel one that never lets a forgiven person come home, and it is especially needed where a leader has fallen.
policies.sample:
RESTORATION POLICY
[Church Name], adopted [Date]

Heart of the Policy
When a person repents, the church's joy is to receive them back, as the father received the prodigal. Restoration is the goal of all discipline.

Restoration to Fellowship
When a person under discipline shows genuine repentance, [the elders / board] confirm it, communicate it to the church as appropriate, and welcome the person back into full fellowship, with the church affirming forgiveness and renewed love.

Rebuilding Trust
Forgiveness is immediate. Trust is rebuilt over time. Where sin caused harm, restoration includes making amends as able, and may include a season of accountability and care agreed with the person.

Restoration of Leaders
A leader who has fallen may be fully restored to fellowship while restoration to a position of leadership or trust is considered separately, prayerfully, and slowly, and is never assumed. Some roles, especially those involving children or finances, may not be restored where the sin involved them, as advised by counsel and safeguarding policy.

Care
Throughout, the church surrounds the person with prayer, support, and honest love, and guards against both harshness and pretending the harm did not happen.

[Where the original matter involved a crime or abuse, follow law and safeguarding policy. Confirm leadership restoration questions with counsel and your insurer.]

closing: Treat every template here as a first draft and nothing more, and adapt each one with your own local legal counsel and your insurance carrier before you adopt it, most of all the safeguarding policies, where the law and a qualified professional must have the final word.
